extracted.intended_audience: students, general readers, and scholars seeking an overview of postcolonial literature
extracted.subtask_description: Identify recurring themes, language practices, stylistic techniques, and political/ideological concerns that define or are used to analyze postcolonial literature across regions and languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern with identity, ethnicity, and language
rubrics_metrics.description: Many West Indian writers share a special concern with questions of identity, ethnicity, and language that rise out of the Caribbean historical experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to evaluate how a work addresses self/collective identity, ethnic difference, and linguistic belonging as shaped by colonial histories; applies broadly across regional postcolonial literatures cited in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dialect/creole (nation language) and code-switching
rubrics_metrics.description: One unique and pervasive characteristic of Caribbean literature is the use of 'dialect' forms of the national language, often termed creole... Many Caribbean authors in their writing switch liberally between the local variation – now commonly termed nation language – and the standard form of the language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the deployment of local varieties (creoles, dialects, 'nation language') and deliberate code-switching between vernacular and standard forms; examples include Earl Lovelace's mixing of Trinidadian dialect patterns and standard English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Themes of exile, diaspora, and questions of national belonging
rubrics_metrics.description: Many writers from former colonies moved to the United Kingdom, the United States, or Canada in order to make a living from their work... critics in their adopted territories might argue that, for instance, V. S. Naipaul ought to be considered a British writer instead of a Trinidadian writer... but most West Indian readers and critics still consider these writers 'West Indian'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the text treats displacement, migration, and competing claims of national/territorial identity (home vs adopted country); consider how exile or long-term residence abroad shapes perspective and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borrowing from oral traditions and folk life
rubrics_metrics.description: By borrowing from and incorporating the non-written oral traditions and folk life of the African diaspora, African-American literature broke 'the mystique of connection between literary authority and patriarchal power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for incorporation of oral storytelling forms, proverbs, folk narratives, and other oral cultural elements that assert alternative literary authority and aesthetic strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political engagement with colonialism, nationalism, and historical events
rubrics_metrics.description: The novels of J. G. Farrell are important texts dealing with the decline of the British Empire... Mahfouz was inspired to write in a large part by his experiences during the Egyptian Revolution of 1919.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether and how the work engages colonial/imperial history, nationalist movements, revolutions, occupation, or the political consequences of empire; examples: Raj Quartet, Farrell's Empire Trilogy, Mahfouz's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Western representation (Orientalism and related critiques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Edward Said published Orientalism, discussing the depiction of Asia by the Western world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion for analyzing how a text challenges, revises, or reproduces Western discourses and stereotypes about colonized peoples; attentive to meta-critical commentary on representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisionist or intertextual 'writing back' to canonical texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea, which was written as a prequel to Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre, deals with themes of women living in a patriarchal society, race, and assimilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate instances where a postcolonial work reimagines, continues, or subverts canonical Western texts to give voice to marginalized characters or perspectives (prequels, sequels, retellings, counter-narratives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid language and stylistic experimentation (magical realism, non-linear narrative, 'bagginess')
rubrics_metrics.description: Amit Chaudhuri feels that after Rushdie, Indian writing in English started employing magical realism, bagginess, non-linear narrative and hybrid language to sustain themes seen as microcosms of India.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for experimental techniques—genre blending, nonlinear structures, hybridity of diction and register, and magical realist elements—used to represent layered postcolonial realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate over authenticity vs imitation and the politics of language choice
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the key issues is the superiority/inferiority of Indian Writing in English (IWE) as opposed to the literary production in the various languages of India. Key polar concepts bandied in this context are superficial/authentic, imitative/creative, shallow/deep, critical/uncritical, elitist/parochial...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating works, consider contested judgments about authenticity, whether writing in a colonial language (e.g., English) is seen as authentic or derivative, and how language choice implicates ideology and audience. The page notes categorization as potentially limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satire and social critique
rubrics_metrics.description: The Singapore Grip is satirical... The story centres on a British family who own one of the colony's leading trading companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the extent to which satire, irony, and comedic inversion are used to critique colonial institutions, bourgeois values, and power structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on gendered experience, race, and assimilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide Sargasso Sea deals with themes of women living in a patriarchal society, race, and assimilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate intersectional attention to gender and race—how colonialism shapes women's lives, racial identities, domestic assimilation, and family structures within postcolonial narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative perspective, moral ambiguity, and generational contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: One recurrent theme is the moral certainty of the older generation as contrasted with the anomie of the younger. Another theme is the treatment of Indians by Britons living in India.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider narrative vantage points, whether the text foregrounds moral certainties or ethical ambiguities, and how generational differences reflect colonial or postcolonial social change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilingualism and promotion of indigenous or minority languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Philippine literature is written in Spanish, English, or any indigenous Philippine languages... R. S. Thomas wanted the Welsh language to be made the official language of Wales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the role assigned to indigenous/minority languages in a work (use, preservation, political advocacy), and how multilingualism functions stylistically and politically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reclaiming literary authority from dominant (colonial) culture
rubrics_metrics.description: In producing their own literature, African Americans were able to establish their own literary traditions devoid of the white intellectual filter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to assess whether a work actively constructs alternative canons, narrative authorities, or aesthetic norms that resist or replace dominant/colonial literary standards.
